job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Nikhil Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thank you for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I wake at seven, make tea, and by eight I'm at the kitchen table at my parents' place in Westbury with two screens. Mornings I apply for jobs and work on a side project, an app that lets neighbours share tools. Afternoons I do a mock interview or help my younger brother with his maths. I use an AI assistant all day, for code, for emails, for explaining things I don't get.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks. What was your degree, and what did you do for your internship?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Computer science with a data focus at Merton University. My final project was a model that predicts bus delays from weather and traffic, built with data from the regional transit authority. I did a ten-week internship there too, mostly cleaning data and building a small dashboard that the planners actually used, which felt great.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's fine, a useful tool among others, and I'd carry on building things with it. Online I'd probably post that hype always comes down to a handful of real use cases.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it means my job hunt stays the main problem, not the technology. Entry-level roles in data near Westbury get hundreds of applicants, and I've got no offer after nine months. It's frustrating, but I have a feel for what the work involves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying and push my side project to a launch, since a real product beats a CV line. I'd answer questions in a developer forum to get noticed. And I'd ask the transit authority planners for a reference and for any contracts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. My money is secure and my family's behind me, so I'm just impatient.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said nine months with no offer. Is that getting to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some days. I'm applying to a lot of roles and a lot of them don't reply at all. I tell myself it's the market, but a rejection note makes a bad evening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you stay motivated?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The side project helps, because I can see people using it. A neighbour told me she borrowed a ladder through it last week, and that kind of thing keeps me going.

Online I'd post that hype usually shrinks to a few real use cases.

do: Push my tool-sharing app to a **real launch**.

Ask the transit authority planners for a **reference** and any contract work.
feel: **Calm**: money is secure and family is behind me, so I'm mostly impatient.

steps.text: Launch the tool-sharing app to 50 neighbours
Ask the transit planners for a reference and contract work
Answer questions on a developer forum each week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exciting if it's handled well, and that governments should make sure the savings reach workers. I'd tell friends to start using the tools now rather than waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think the junior coding work, the small tasks I'd be hired for, is the first stuff that moves to software. So fewer entry posts, and the ones left want someone who can steer the tools. That's fine for me, I do that daily, but it makes the gap wider.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for roles where I manage and check AI output, and I'd put my daily workflow on show with a short video. I'd also apply to the transit authority's data team and maybe start contracting on small freelance jobs. I'd teach my brother and a couple of friends how to use the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'll be okay, but I can see friends who won't be, and that sits in my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who around you worries you most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My friend Callum, a graphic design graduate who refuses to use these tools. He's good, but he thinks it's cheating. I think he'll lose clients and I don't know how to say it kindly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you charge for freelance work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe thirty pounds an hour at first, small data cleaning jobs. It's not much, but it proves people will pay me, and that's worth more than the money.

I'd tell friends to start using the tools **now**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is quick, but I'd say we should treat it as the biggest policy question in a lifetime. I'd push for free training and income support and say it loudly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it's the one that makes me think properly. My degree is thinking work, so I'd be in the first wave, but I'd also be better placed than most because I'm already working with the tools. The robots for hands-on work come about 2031, so some people get a little more time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any decent data or software job I can get, fast. I'd save most of what I earn, and I'd start learning about robotics and control systems, since that's where the human side meets the machine. I'd also help my parents plan their money, because Dad's close to retiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm not scared for myself as much as for my family and friends, but yes, it's heavy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're better placed than most. Does that change what you owe anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It makes me feel I should help, yes. I'd run free sessions for people at the library on how to use the tools. If I'm ahead by luck, I should share it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries you about your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dad's pension is invested in funds that would swing wildly. I'd want him to move some into safer places before 2028, and he's stubborn about it.

say: Two years is quick, so I'd call it the biggest **policy question** in a lifetime.
I'd push for free training and **income support**.
think: My degree is thinking work, so I'd be in the **first wave**, but ahead of most.
Robots reach hands-on work about **2031**, so some people get more time.
do: Take any decent data or software job **fast**.

Help my parents move some pension money somewhere **safer**.
feel: **Anxious**, mostly for family and friends, and it's heavy.
S2.quote: If I'm ahead by luck, I should share it.
fieldNote: **Anxiety** is about family and peers more than his own skills.
Sees his head start as luck and offers free library **sessions**.
Wants his father to **de-risk** a pension before 2028.

steps.text: Take the first decent data or software job offered
Save two-thirds of my pay in a safe account
Study robotics control systems in evenings
Help Dad move part of his pension into safer funds

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to get a handle on it. I'd say the right response is to build training and safety nets now, with unions at the table, not after the damage is done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's mostly an opportunity, if I'm honest. I'd have time for a few good jobs and to build something of my own. The part I worry about is how fast the thinking work turns over around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a solid first job, learn how a real team ships software, and keep the side project alive. By year three I'd aim at a startup or a small co-operative that builds tools for communities. And I'd put aside a fixed amount every month into an index fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but optimistic. There's time and I like having an angle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a co-operative. Is that a serious plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a plan with a question mark. I'd want to try it with two friends for a year, and if it's not paying our rent by then, I'd go back to a normal job. But it's an experiment I'd actually like to run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you say to people who think this is naive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's fair, but the other option is to wait until someone else decides for you, and I'd prefer to have a hand in it.

say: Five years is enough to get a handle on it, with **unions** at the table.
Training and safety nets should come **before** the damage.
think: For me it's mostly an **opportunity**, with time for a few good jobs.
I worry about how fast thinking work turns over around **2031**.
do: Take a solid **first job** and learn how a real team ships software.

feel: **Uneasy** but optimistic: there's time, and I have an angle.
S3.quote: The other option is to wait until someone else decides for you, and I'd prefer to have a hand in it.

steps.text: Take a solid first software job at a team that ships weekly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years feels almost generous, and I'd say so while still pushing for proper public training. The danger is people thinking they have all the time in the world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's plenty of time. I'd be 33, maybe running my own small company or leading a team, and by then these tools will be like electricity. I'd be more interested in what we use them for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the usual: first job, a couple of promotions, side projects. I'd maybe do a part-time master's in AI ethics and policy, because I'd like to help shape rules. And I'd save for a flat in Westbury so I'm not paying rent when things shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. I'm curious more than anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in the first year of that decade, specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get hired, buy a decent second-hand laptop for the side project, and join a local tech meet-up. And I'd start a savings pot that I don't touch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you worry about being too relaxed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. Relaxed is good for me, but a country that's relaxed for nine years has a bad tenth.

The danger is people thinking they have **all the time** in the world.

I'm more interested in what we use the tools **for**.

Do a part-time **master's** in AI ethics and policy.
S4.quote: A country that's relaxed for nine years has a bad tenth.
fieldNote: Time makes him calm and moves his **thinking** to policy.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, by a margin, but even that feels more like a puzzle than a disaster for me. What worries me is people around me who haven't touched these tools. What would help is public training that's free, plus rules that make companies share what they gain.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that I'm lucky. I know that. My parents back me, I have no debt and I like this stuff, so I'm not the typical person in these scenarios.

headlineQuote: My parents back me, I have no debt and I like this stuff, so I'm not the typical person in these scenarios.
portrait: Nikhil is a **23-year-old** computer science graduate living with his parents, still waiting for his first offer after several months.
He is **progressive** and backs unions, regulation and public support, and he thinks companies should share what AI saves them.
He uses **AI tools** every day, builds side projects and sees change as a puzzle rather than a threat.
His mood stays **calm** or uneasy until the 2028 world, where he turns anxious, mainly about the people around him.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture, mostly for the people who have never touched these tools.
whatWouldHelp: Free **public training** and rules that make companies **share** what they gain.
